newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Down home bourbon wins new fans in cities.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Down home bourbon wins new fans in cities.

text.p: Bourbon, the down home drink of the South, is making a resurgence far from the bluegrass of Kentucky in the restaurants and clubs of New York.

"Bourbon really left the scene except in the Deep South, except in William Faulkner's mind," Bill Samuels, president of the Maker's Mark distillery, said at a recent tasting in a trendy Manhattan restaurant.
Now bourbon, whose roots reach back to the earliest days of the republic, is attracting attention among a younger, urban crowd, many of them women and "North of the Mason-Dixon line," Samuels says.

"I see it from Miami up to Boston," and particularly in the Northeast, said Samuels, a seventh generation distiller whose family's roots in Kentucky whiskey go back to 1780. "For them, bourbon is new. It wasn't their father's drink."

The new devotees, however, have set their sights on the very best, the speciality bourbons such as Heaven Hill's Elijah Craig, Jim Beam's Knob Creek and Maker's Mark, the smallest of the bourbon distilleries. The Maker's Mark distillery is located a few miles outside the small town of Loretto, Ky.
Samuels, a tall, plain-spoken man, introduces himself by saying, "I'm from Kentucky and I make bourbon whiskey."
For anyone who may have missed the point, he starts off a historical and gustatory journey of bourbon by saying, "We're going to drink some whiskey, whether you want to or not."

Bourbon was born out of necessity during Kentucky's frontier days just after the American Revolution. Farmers found that the easiest way to bring their corn to market was in distilled form as whiskey.
The region also was blessed with iron-free water from limestone formations and a plentiful supply of white oak to make the barrels to hold the whiskey.

"The miracle of Kentucky is corn, water and wood," Samuels said. He noted that the 12 bourbon distillers are within a limited geologic zone extending from around Louisville, Ky., to Tennessee, where Jack Daniels is made.

Bourbon is aged in barrels that have been charred inside. This give the whiskey its colour. After the barrels have been used once they are exported to Scotland, where most Scotch whisky is aged in used bourbon barrels, Samuels said.
Distillers need to get the perfect correlation between wood flavor and whiskey, he said. This means that the bourbon is generally aged for about six years.
"This is just the way our whiskey is designed so that the alcohol flavor is blended and balanced with the tannins in the wood. It's all about achieving balance."

While Scotch whiskies may be aged far longer, Samuels noted that the use of newly charred barrels causes bourbon to mature faster. He also said Scotland's colder weather inhibits the maturation process.

The six-year ageing period still means that bourbon's resurgence has given distillers of speciality brands an enviable problem -- demand is rising faster than supply, not only in the United States, but also overseas.
Exports will account for about 20 percent of the distillery's sales this year, Samuels said, adding: "Ten years ago it was zero."
The export demand was led by the Japanese and spread to Australia, London and Paris. "That was just a few years ahead of this emergence in the U.S., the East Coast," he said.
For Maker's Mark, the demand growth meant that by late October the company had stopped taking new orders for the year. It expects to sell about 275,000 cases this year.
"Overall our growth is about 11 or 12 percent, which is all the whiskey there is. It would be higher, but we haven't got it." Samuels said.
Behind the growth in demand for speciality bourbon and single malt Scotch is a trend toward carefully crafted, local products and away from mass-produced items.
"The enjoyment in malt whiskey, like speciality bourbon, is in experimenting," Samuels said.
And the best way to enjoy bourbon? An ounce of bourbon and about a half an ounce of distilled water.
